summary: Describes how clients of the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) can authenticate using OpenID Connect, so one login at an identity provider can be used with many RDAP servers. This lets servers make access control decisions based on who the client is, without a separate account at each server.

eli5.summary: Instead of showing a different ID card at every door, you show one trusted card. This lets users log in once and look up domain owner information at many places.

questions: how does federated login work for rdap
subtitle: One login at a trusted identity provider, usable with many RDAP servers, so registries can decide who sees what.

tldr.problem: RDAP servers can decide how much registration data to show based on who is asking, but making users get a separate username and password from hundreds of server operators does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: RDAP servers outsource login to OpenID Connect identity providers. Clients either let the server run the login and keep a session cookie, or run it themselves and send an access token with each query. Two new claims and two query parameters carry the purpose of a query and a do-not-track request.
tldr.outcome: A server can make fine-grained access decisions from identity information released with the user's consent. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and registers the extension identifier farv1.

today: RFC 9560 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Problem With Per-Server Logins
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) provides RESTful web services for retrieving registration data from domain name and regional internet registries. RDAP lets a server make access control decisions based on who the client is, and it relies on the client identification features of HTTP. RFC 7481 describes identification and authentication services that can be used with RDAP, but it does not say how to use them.

The RFC argues that the conventional username and password model does not scale. If every domain and address registry offers RDAP, it is impractical for users to get credentials from hundreds of server operators. Passwords also tell a server little about the user, while protecting the user's privacy, so operators cannot make fine-grained decisions.

The approach is federation. A user with an identifier from a recognized provider gets a basic level of service. Users who need more can get identifiers from specialized providers that can describe them in more detail, and share that information with the server with their consent. The RFC builds this on OpenID Connect.
sections.eli5: Imagine needing a separate library card for every library in the world. This RFC lets you carry one trusted card that every library can check.

sections.title: How RDAP Uses OpenID Connect
sections.content:
OpenID Connect is a single sign-on system built on the OAuth 2.0 framework. Users get identifiers from OpenID Providers (OPs). Applications that outsource login to an OP are Relying Parties (RPs). Here, RDAP servers can form a federation, and a client can use one credential registered with any OP in that federation.

The RFC defines two kinds of client. A session-oriented client, such as a web browser querying a server directly, hands the OpenID Connect work to the RDAP server and keeps the session with an HTTP cookie. A token-oriented client, such as JavaScript run from a web service, talks to the OP itself and sends an access token to the server, which acts as a resource server. Clients MAY act as either type but MUST NOT mix the two while interacting with an OP. Servers SHOULD support both but MAY support only one.

The server's OP can be a default OP, used when the client names none, or a remote OP chosen by the client with an end-user identifier or an Issuer Identifier. A server must support at least one method of OP discovery.

The flow for a session-oriented client starts with a help query. The rdapConformance value farv1 signals support for this extension. The server then redirects the client to the OP, the OP authenticates the user and obtains consent, and the server swaps the returned authorization code for an ID Token and access token and retrieves the user's claims.
sections.eli5: The library asks you to go to the card office. The card office checks who you are, asks if you are happy to share your details, and then tells the library what it needs to know.

sections.title: Claims, Query Parameters and Configuration
sections.content:
The RDAP-specific claims are tied to an OAuth scope value of rdap. The rdap_allowed_purposes claim is an array of case-sensitive strings naming the purposes for which a user may request protected data, such as a law enforcement agent or a trademark attorney asserting a legal right to access. Servers MUST ignore unrecognized purpose values, and identity providers MUST only assign purposes to identities authorized to use them. The rdap_dnt_allowed claim is a JSON boolean. If it is true, the user is authenticated and authorized, and local regulations allow it, the server MUST NOT log, track or record the association between query and user.

Two optional query parameters go with RDAP queries for protected resources. farv1_qp carries one query purpose. The server SHOULD check it against the user's allowed purposes and MUST return HTTP 403 if the purpose is not allowed. farv1_dnt carries true or false, and the server MUST return HTTP 403 if it cannot do what the parameter asks. Unrecognized parameters MUST be ignored, and queries with identification tied to an unsupported OP MUST be rejected with HTTP 400.

A server describes itself in the farv1_openidcConfiguration object of its help response. Required members say whether session clients, token clients and do-not-track are supported. Optional members cover provider discovery, explicit Issuer Identifiers, implicit token refresh and a list of supported OPs, one of which may be marked as the default. A server MUST set at least one of the session or token client flags to true.
sections.eli5: You can write on your request why you want to look, like "homework". You can also ask the librarian not to write down that you came, but only people allowed to ask that will get a yes.

sections.title: Sessions for Session-Oriented Clients
sections.content:
Session-oriented clients use new path segments that start with farv1_session/. login starts a session and the server sets an HTTP cookie that the client MUST send on later requests. status reports on the session, refresh extends it and logout ends it. A second login that includes a cookie gets HTTP 409. So do status, refresh or logout sent without a session cookie. A query whose session has expired gets HTTP 401.

The user is named with the farv1_id query parameter or an HTTP Basic authorization header carrying the identifier with no password. The OP can be named with farv1_iss. Login responses are valid RDAP responses containing a farv1_session object with the user ID, issuer, claims and a sessionInfo object holding tokenExpiration in seconds and tokenRefresh.

For clients with limited user interfaces, such as curl or wget, device and devicepoll use the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628). The server returns a farv1_deviceInfo object with a user code and a verification URI. The user types the code into a browser on a second device while the server polls the OP.

On logout, tokens can be revoked if the OP supports it, and the server SHOULD invalidate the cookie. Without a logout, the server MUST end the session after a server-defined time.
sections.eli5: When you check in you get a wristband. You show it at every room, you can swap it for a new one, and you hand it back when you leave. If it expires, you need to check in again.

sections.title: Tokens for Token-Oriented Clients
sections.content:
A token-oriented client logs the user in with the OP directly, appending any additionalAuthorizationQueryParams from the server's configuration to the authorization request. The OP SHOULD put the RDAP server's client_id in the aud claim of the ID Token. The client then sends the access token in an HTTP Authorization header using the bearer scheme. If the token came from a remote OP, the client MUST also include farv1_iss with the Issuer Identifier. This section defines no new data structures or parameters for these clients.

The server MUST validate the token before using it for access control, either by token introspection with the issuing OP or by examining a JWT access token. It MAY then fetch the user's claims from the OP and MAY cache validated information until the token expires. A client SHOULD watch token expiry and refresh as needed.

A token may have an aud value that does not include the server's own client ID, for example when a client acts as a proxy. The server might not trust it, but it can exchange the token with the OP for trusted tokens using OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693).
sections.eli5: Here you carry your own ticket from the card office and show it at the door. The librarian checks that the ticket is real and not out of date before letting you in.

sections.title: Registrations and Purpose Values
sections.content:
IANA registered farv1 in the RDAP Extensions registry, with the intended usage of federated authentication for RDAP version 1 using OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect. It also registered the claims rdap_allowed_purposes and rdap_dnt_allowed in the JSON Web Token Claims registry.

A new registry holds RDAP query purpose values, operated under the Specification Required policy. Values may use only ASCII letters and the underscore and must be 1 to 64 characters long. The initial values come from the final report of the Expert Working Group on gTLD Directory Services and range from domainNameControl and legalActions to criminalInvestigationAndDNSAbuseMitigation and dnsTransparency.
sections.eli5: The rule book gets a new page listing the official reasons you can give for looking something up. Each reason has a short name and a plain description.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of RDAP (RFC 7481), OpenID Connect Core and OAuth 2.0. When TLS is used, the practices in RFC 9325 MUST be followed. The OAuth 2.0 Implicit Flow is considered insecure, and it MUST NOT be used.

Fields such as userClaims can be personally identifiable. Server operators must have policies so that such data is disclosed only to clients authorized to receive it.

The do-not-track claim depends on the good will of the server and its proxies, so it needs out-of-band trust. If accepted, the resulting information loss could seriously impair audit capabilities.

Access control policy is left to each operator. For example, a client giving only an email address might see a subset of what a client giving an email address, a full name and a stated purpose would see.
sections.eli5: Treat the information on your card like a secret. Only share it with people who are allowed to see it. Telling the librarian not to write your name down only works if you trust the librarian.
